{{Short description|Conservation scientist (1926–2017)}}
<!--When you move this draft into article space, please link it to the Wikidata entry and remove the QID in the infobox code.--> {{Infobox person/Wikidata|fetchwikidata=ALL|dateformat=mdy}}

'''Elisabeth West FitzHugh''' (born July 30, 1926 – January 13, 2017) was a Lebanese American conservation scientist. She was a fellow of the [[American Institute for Conservation]] and the [[International Institute for Conservation]].

== Early life and education ==
Elisabeth West FitzHugh ([[Birth name#Maiden and married names|née]] Hebard West) was born on July 30, 1926, in [[Beirut]], Lebanon, where her father William A. West was a professor of Chemistry. She attended primary school there at the [[American Community School Beirut]]. She was an undergraduate student in chemistry at [[Vassar College]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2017-01-27|title=Obituary for Elisabeth FitzHugh|url=https://washingtonconservationguild.org/2017/01/27/obituary-elisabeth-fitzhugh/|access-date=2022-01-23|website=Washington Conservation Guild|language=en-US}}</ref> After earning her bachelor's degree, she moved to the [[UCL Institute of Archaeology]] (then [[University of London]]), where she earned a master's degree in the Archaeology of Western Asia.{{cn|date=January 2022}} During her studies, she worked as an assistant curator and librarian at the [[American University of Beirut]]. She visited the [[Oriental Institute (Chicago)|Oriental Institute]] on an archaeological expedition in October 1950.<ref name=":0"/> On returning to the United States, FitzHugh met with [[George M. A. Hanfmann]], then curator of the [[Fogg Art Museum]], to discuss her career.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Harmon|first=Dr Elizabeth|date=2021-07-06|title=Elisabeth West FitzHugh, a Driving Force in Cultural Heritage Conservation and Scientific Research|url=https://siarchives.si.edu/blog/elisabeth-west-fitzhugh-driving-force-cultural-heritage-conservation-and-scientific-research|access-date=2022-01-23|website=Smithsonian Institution Archives|language=en}}</ref> He recommended that she speak to [[Rutherford John Gettens]] at the [[Smithsonian Institution]].<ref name=":1"/>

== Career ==
FitzHugh was appointed to the technical research team at the [[Freer Gallery of Art]] in 1956. She worked alongside Gettens to establish a technical scientific laboratory at the art gallery, creating the protocols for the analysis of materials and pigments.<ref name=":0"/> Specifically, she developed the laboratory procedures to better understand the Chinese bronzes.<ref name=":0"/> This involved wet chemistry approaches and emission spectroscopy.<ref name=":1"/> FitzHugh had access to primitative characterization equipment at the Freer Gallery, including chemical, comparison and metallurgical microscopes.<ref name=":1"/> To perform [[X-ray diffraction]] measurements, she visited the [[National Museum of Natural History]].<ref name=":1"/>

FitzHugh spent her entire career at the Freer Gallery, working as an analytical and conservation scientist. She was identified by Dr Joyce Hill Stoner as the first woman cultural heritage scientist at the Smithsonian.<ref name=":1" /> She soon became an expert in Chinese Jade and bronze, Japanese painting and oriental lacquer. Amongst the many artists' pigments studied by FitzHugh, her work on the chemistry of [[Han purple and Han blue]] were groundbreaking.<ref name=":0"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=FitzHugh|first1=Elisabeth West|last2=Zycherman|first2=Lynda A.|date=1992|title=A Purple Barium Copper Silicate Pigment from Early China|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1506342|journal=Studies in Conservation|volume=37|issue=3|pages=145–154|doi=10.2307/1506342|jstor=1506342 |issn=0039-3630|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=FitzHugh|first1=Elisabeth West|last2=Zycherman|first2=Lynda A.|date=1983-02-01|title=An early man-made blue pigment from China—barium copper silicate|url=https://doi.org/10.1179/sic.1983.28.1.15|journal=Studies in Conservation|volume=28|issue=1|pages=15–23|doi=10.1179/sic.1983.28.1.15|issn=0039-3630|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

FitzHugh was interested in the conservation and protection of art.<ref name=":0"/> She served as editor of ''International Institute for Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works (IIC) Abstracts'', a journal summarizing the abstracts of books, conference proceedings and dissertations on art, archaeology and architecture.<ref>{{Cite web|title=AATA Online Abstracts of International Conservation Literature {{!}} Princeton University Library|url=https://library.princeton.edu/resource/4529|access-date=2022-01-23|website=library.princeton.edu}}</ref> She held various roles in the [[American Institute for Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works]], including Chair of Ethics and Standards and eventually President.<ref name=":0"/>

== Awards and honors ==
* 1990: [[American Institute for Conservation]] R. J. Gettens Award<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gettens Award|url=https://www.culturalheritage.org/membership/awards/gettens-award|access-date=2022-01-23|website=www.culturalheritage.org}}</ref>
* 1992: Honorary member of the American Institute for Conservation<ref>{{Cite web|title=Honorary Membership|url=https://www.culturalheritage.org/membership/awards/honorary-membership|access-date=2022-01-23|website=www.culturalheritage.org}}</ref>
* 2002: [[International Institute for Conservation]] of Historic and Artistic Works Forbes Prize<ref>{{Cite web|title=Forbes Prize Lecture {{!}} International Institute for Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works|url=https://www.iiconservation.org/forbesprize|access-date=2022-01-23|website=www.iiconservation.org|archive-date=2022-01-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220123222223/https://www.iiconservation.org/forbesprize|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2016: Honorary fellow of the International Institute for Conservation<ref>{{Cite web|title=Honorary Fellows of IIC {{!}} International Institute for Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works|url=https://www.iiconservation.org/node/12|access-date=2022-01-23|website=www.iiconservation.org|archive-date=2022-01-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220123222211/https://www.iiconservation.org/node/12|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
FitzHugh retired in 1991, but continued to work at the Smithsonian until 2011. She died in 2017 in [[Mitchellville, Maryland]].<ref name=":0"/>

Her personal collection of conservation volumes was donated posthumously to the [[South African Institute for Heritage Science and Conservation]], and form the core of the collection housed there at the Elisabeth FitzHugh Conservation Library

== Family ==
FitzHugh was married to Richard FitzHugh, a biophysicist at the [[National Institutes of Health]].{{cn|date=February 2024}}
